title: Cooperative Suppression and Accelerator Exclusion on Copper: Mechanistic Origin of Thiadiazole Leveler G1 for Blind-Microvia Superfilling in Acidic Sulfate Plating.
summary: High-density interconnection (HDI) printed circuit boards require precise defect control during copper microvia electrodeposition, where levelers play a decisive role in defining the filling window and deposit quality. This work investigates 2-amino-5-mercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole (G1) as a leveler and compares it with the structurally analogous 2,5-diamino-1,3,4-thiadiazole (G2) to clarify the relationship between molecular structure, interfacial adsorption regulation, and microvia superfilling. Microvia plating experiments, electrochemical characterization, density functional theory (DFT), and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were combined to reveal the distinct behaviors of G1 and G2. Plating results show that only G1 enables bottom-up superfilling of blind microvias while maintaining low surface roughness and a preferred Cu(220) orientation. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that G1 exhibits strong cooperative suppression with the suppressor PEP and effectively resists competitive adsorption by the accelerator ZPS, forming a highly inhibiting PEP-ZPS-G1 system with a measurable convection response. In contrast, G2 shows weak synergy with PEP and lacks comparable electrochemical features, explaining its inferior filling performance. DFT calculations indicate that the asymmetric substitution of G1 produces a more heterogeneous charge distribution and enhanced active sites, strengthening its interactions with the cathodic interface and coadditives. MD simulations further confirm that G1 adsorbs more stably on Cu(111), increases PEP surface coverage, and suppresses effective ZPS adsorption, leading to selective interfacial regulation characterized by strong PEP adsorption and weak ZPS adsorption. These results establish a clear structure-function relationship for thiadiazole-based levelers and provide guidance for rational molecular design in advanced copper electrodeposition.

screen.tldr: DFT and MD explain why a thiadiazole additive enables copper microvia superfilling by cooperative adsorption with suppressor and accelerator species.
screen.transfer_note: Interfacial adsorption analysis could inform additive design and surface-competition modeling for crystal growth control in materials processing.

title: A generalized Knudsen theory for gas transport in disordered porous materials.
summary: Gas transport through nanoporous materials is central to membrane separations, catalysis, and energy technologies. Predicting permeability in these materials is crucial for performance evaluation and material design, but their complex porous network poses significant challenges. Here, we develop a generalized theoretical framework for Knudsen flow in random porous materials. We further derive a concise permeability equation dependent solely on two measurable structural parameters: mean pore size and porosity. Monte Carlo simulations across 5000 random porous networks with porosities ranging from 0 to 0.8 validate the theory with R2 = 0.985. Non-equilibrium molecular dynamics simulations confirm the applicability of the theory to porous membrane materials, including polymers of intrinsic microporosity, polyamide, and zeolitic imidazolate frameworks. By accounting for molecular size effects, we extend the framework to predict gas selectivity in materials with sub-nanometer pores, showing good agreement with experimental data for weakly adsorbing gases. This work extends Knudsen theory to random porous networks and molecular-sized pores, providing a practical and accessible tool for predicting gas permeability and selectivity in nanoporous materials.

screen.tldr: Generalized Knudsen-flow theory predicts gas permeability and selectivity in random nanoporous materials from pore size and porosity, validated by simulations and experiments.

title: Dual-Ion Cl-/Zn2+ Storage in a π-Conjugated Indanthrone Cathode for Aqueous Zinc Batteries.
summary: Conventional aqueous zinc batteries rely almost exclusively on Zn2+ insertion reactions, limiting reaction diversity and often causing structural instability. Here we show that a π-conjugated indanthrone molecular crystal enables an unusual dual-ion Cl-/Zn2+ storage mechanism in aqueous electrolyte. The IDT lattice combines carbonyl redox sites with π-stacked channels that allow anion interaction within the conjugated framework. Electrochemical and spectroscopic analyses reveal that Zn2+ coordinates with carbonyl oxygen sites during discharge in the low-voltage region (0.4-1.4 V), while oxidation at higher potentials (1.6-1.8 V) is compensated by reversible uptake of Cl- within the π-conjugated lattice. Ex situ XRD, Raman, and XPS measurements consistently support this direction-dependent ion participation. The IDT framework undergoes only small and reversible lattice variations during cycling, enabling stable operation in aqueous electrolytes. This work establishes a molecular-crystal strategy for enabling cation-anion coupled storage in aqueous batteries, expanding the reaction chemistry of zinc systems beyond conventional Zn2+-dominated insertion mechanisms.

screen.tldr: π-Conjugated indanthrone molecular crystal enables reversible dual-ion Cl−/Zn2+ storage in aqueous zinc batteries with small lattice changes and stable cycling.

title: A Computational Investigation of Site Preferential Cation Occupation in High Entropy Spinel Oxide Electrocatalysts for Oxygen Evolution Reaction
summary: High entropy spinel oxides (HESOs) have shown enhanced electrocatalytic performance towards the oxygen evolution reaction (OER), enabled by tunable electronic structures via multi-cation engineering. However, understanding and controlling site-specific cation distributions remains a key challenge. While it is commonly assumed that equimolar mixing of metal precursors will yield a uniform distribution of cations among sites, advanced experimental characterization techniques like XAS demonstrate that the tetrahedral and octahedral sites present in spinel oxides have notably different distributions of elements. We take advantage of elemental site preference to dope a Co-Fe-Cr-Mn-Ni spinel framework with a sixth cation of strong tetrahedral site preference energy, Zn. Our previous work developed a local impurity HESO model for the five-element system [1]; here, we build upon this model using density functional theory to confirm the site preference of Zn and determine its impact on the other elements in the system. We subsequently develop a new fully high entropy model of the six-element system to clearly determine the coordination states and site preferences of all cations. Finally, we calculate the OER activity of various HESO active sites and the effect of Zn inclusion on the system, finding that an increased occupancy of Co 3+ and Co 2+ in octahedral sites in Zn-HESO compared to the pristine HESO leads to more available active sites for OER and increased electrical conductivity, with good agreement with our experimental results [2]. Our computational results demonstrate that adding a selected cation effectively tunes coordination site occupation in spinels, showing a clear structure-property relationship and providing a clue for the development of next-generation multicomponent catalysts. [1] Baek, J.; Hossain, M.D.; Mukherjee, P. et al. Synergistic effects of mixing and strain in high entropy spinel oxides for oxygen evolution reaction. Nat Commun 14 , 5936 (2023). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-023-41359-7 [2] Baek, J.; Hamkins, K. S.; Li, Y.; et al. Modulating Coordinate Site Occupancy in High-entropy Spinel Electrocatalysts. (under review)

screen.tldr: DFT study of cation site preference and OER activity in high-entropy spinel oxides, showing Zn doping reshapes octahedral/tetrahedral occupancy and catalytic behavior.

title: Multiscale investigation of single-vacancy defects in 2D C60 crystals.
summary: The recent synthesis of two-dimensional C60 crystals (2D C60) has unveiled a new class of carbon semiconductors with tunable bandgaps and exceptional thermal stability. While the perfect properties of 2D C60 have been extensively characterized, the impact of intrinsic defects, which is inevitable in practical applications, remains largely unexplored. In this study, we systematically investigated the stability, magnetism, electronic, and mechanic properties of all 16 single-vacancy defects in 2D C60 using first-principles calculations, followed by a multiscale analysis of their mechanical response via a machine learning neuroevolution potential (NEP). Our study reveals multiple physical effects induced by single-vacancy defects in 2D C60. We found that the lattice reconstruction stabilizes the defect thermodynamically but leads to bandgap closure and metallization. Rich magnetic properties including non-magnetic, ferromagnetic and anti-ferromagnetic states can be induced by the vacancy defects. We also found pronounced anisotropy and a generally degradation of ideal strength, with no direct correlation observed between thermodynamic stability and mechanical integrity. Furthermore, using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations, we found a critical temperature-dependent failure mechanism. This work provides theoretical support for defect engineering in 2D C60 and paves the way for its practical applications.

screen.tldr: First-principles and NEP simulations study single-vacancy defects in 2D C60, showing reconstruction, metallization, magnetism, and degraded anisotropic mechanical strength.

title: Porphyrin-Based MOFs on Au(111) Vs. Graphene: Comparing Structural, Electronic and Magnetic Properties
summary: Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), composed of organic building blocks linked to metal atoms, are typically characterized by their large pores and low densities. These properties make them excellent candidates for a wide range of applications, ranging from gas storage to catalysis and even multiferroics. The two-dimensional limit of MOFs is typically called metal-organic coordination network (MOCN). Since the MOCN requires a support substrate, its properties are often altered due to the interaction with the latter. For preserving as well as studying the (functional) properties, a decoupling layer between (metallic) substrate and MOCN is required. Graphene, due to its chemical inertness and the low density of states near the Fermi level, has been shown to be a good choice as a decoupling layer. Moreover, it offers the possibility to make use of the full surface science tool kit to obtain fundamental information about structural, electronic and magnetic properties. Herein, we report on the investigation of a MOCN composed of cyanophenyl-functionalized Co-porphyrin (CoTCPP) molecules and Co atoms on both Au(111) [1] and graphene/Ir(111) and compare it to the properties of the H-bonded phases on the same substrates (see Figure 1). With scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) we studied the structural properties, while scanning tunneling spectroscopy and photoelectron spectroscopy measurements were used to determine the electronic properties. For both the H-bonded phase and the MOCN the formation of an interface state was observed on Au(111), but not on graphene. Kondo and X-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements indicated a variation in spin-substrate coupling with bonding motif, and variations in magnetic moment and spin distribution. These results highlight the importance of the bonding motif within supramolecular architectures, and the role of the substrate, in preserving/ tuning the electronic as well as magnetic properties. [1] B.D. Baker Cortes et al., J. Phys. Chem. C 123 (2019) 19681; B.D. Baker Cortes et al., J. Phys. Chem. C 125 (2021) 24557. Figure 1: STM images showing the (a) H-bonded, (b) the threefold and (c) the fourfold Co-coordinated arrangements of CoTCPP molecules on Au(111). The unit cell is depicted in red while an individual molecule is highlighted by the yellow outline. Image sizes: (a) 7.5 nm x 7.5 nm, (b) 17 nm x 17 nm, (c) 7.5 nm x 7.5 nm. Figure 1

screen.tldr: Surface-science study comparing porphyrin-based MOF/MOCN phases on Au(111) and graphene, focusing on substrate-dependent structure, electronic behavior, and magnetism.
